the Marcus theory is valid even in the inverted region for the electron donor-acceptors studied here, but that electron-vibration coulings are crucial to understand charge recombination kinetics in the inversion region.
the charge-recombination rate of electron donor- and acceptor-conjugates can be tuned over 10 orders of magnitude by variation of the acceptor strength, the length of the linker and the solvent.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a novel type of donor-acceptor chromophore systems with tunable electron-acceptor strengths and rigid spacers.
the development of a new class of electron-donor/acceptor conjugates that allow us to investigate the Marcus theory for charge separation and recombination in the inverted region.
a systematic investigation of a series of electron-acceptor chromophores and their conjugates with a porphyrin donor.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Marcus curves are not universal but depend on the nature of the donor-acceptor systems and the experimental conditions, which has been known for decades but is rarely discussed in the literature.
the Marcus curves are not only dependent on the donor and acceptor strength, but also on the nature of the spacer.
the electron-transfer rates in the inverted regime are determined by electron-vibration coupling rather than by the reorganization energy, as predicted by Marcus theory.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the electron-vibration coulings, which are not taken into account in Marcus theory, play an important role in the electron-transfer kinetics in the inverted regime.

the charge-recombination rates are not simply a function of the free energies of the electron-transfer reactions, but are also strongly influenced by the electronic coupling between donor and acceptor.
the Marcus curves for the electron-transfer reactions are strongly affected by the electron acceptor strength and the solvent.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Marcus curves are highly sensitive to subtle changes in the donor and acceptor, and that they can be tuned to cover an exceptionally wide range of reorganization energies.
the electron-vibration coupling is a key factor in the Marcus theory that needs to be considered in order to obtain reliable charge-recombination kinetics.
the Marcus curve is not only a function of the driving force and the reorganization energy but also of the electronic and vibrational structure of the electron donor-accepter conjugate.
